edges.description: The drug occupies the cardiac fast sodium channel. This is the lesion the class is dangerous for.
The same molecules inhibit the rapid delayed-rectifier potassium current that repolarizes the ventricle.
Tricyclics are alpha-1 antagonists at the concentrations reached in overdose.
Tricyclics compete with acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors with sub-micromolar potency.
The class's therapeutic action - transporter blockade - persists in overdose and contributes to the cardiovascular picture.
Central drug accumulation plus histamine H1 blockade produces sedation that deepens with dose.

Seizures are a recognised consequence of the exposure, but the responsible receptor action is not settled - which is why this link is typed UNKNOWN rather than being routed through a named receptor node.
Loss of the sodium current depresses the phase 0 upstroke, so the action potential departs from its normal configuration without the resting potential moving.
The same loss of depolarizing current weakens excitation-contraction coupling, so the pump fails alongside the conduction system.
Slow and spatially heterogeneous conduction is the classical substrate for reentry.
The widened QRS complex is the direct surface recording of the slowed intraventricular conduction.
Conduction slowing at the atrioventricular node and below produces block.
Disproportionate slowing in the right bundle and right ventricular outflow tract gives the Brugada configuration described in this poisoning.
Loss of the repolarizing current lengthens the action potential, the other direction in which this poisoning deforms it.
A smaller, slower phase 0 upstroke propagates more slowly through conducting tissue and working myocardium.
The repolarization arm of the same action-potential change.

Perfusion failure that outruns fluid, sodium loading and vasopressors ends in arrest without needing a rhythm event to get there. This is the second route to the arrest node, alongside the reentrant one.
Perfusion failure produces anaerobic metabolism and lactate accumulation. The intermediate steps are standard shock physiology rather than anything specific to this poison.

Acidaemia deepens the channel blockade that produced it. This is the one edge in the entry that points back upstream, and it is drawn deliberately - the vicious cycle is why deterioration in this poisoning is abrupt rather than gradual.
The ingestion is the route by which the systemic drug burden is established. Everything else in the entry is downstream of it.

edges.description: The model is defined by the conduction defect: animals were dosed until the QRS exceeded 120 ms, and QRS duration is the primary electrocardiographic outcome.
edges.limitations: Toxicity is produced by controlled intravenous infusion to an electrocardiographic endpoint rather than by ingestion, so absorption kinetics, co-ingestants and the time course of a real overdose are absent.

edges.description: The same dosing endpoint includes profound hypotension, and systolic pressure after treatment is the model's other primary outcome.

edges.description: The model is defined by a haemodynamic endpoint and reads out mean arterial pressure and cardiac output continuously.
edges.limitations: Mortality was high enough in both arms that the authors describe the study as a pilot, so a null result here does not exclude a smaller effect.
edges.source: Amitriptyline-infusion swine model of tricyclic-induced hypotension

edges.description: QRS duration lengthens significantly in every amitriptyline-treated group, so the conduction defect is reproduced.
edges.limitations: Rodent ventricular repolarization is carried by a different set of potassium currents from the human ventricle, so the QTc arm of this model translates poorly and the hERG limb of the human lesion is not usefully represented. Treatment is given simultaneously with the poison rather than after toxicity appears, which is not the clinical situation.
edges.source: Intraperitoneal amitriptyline rat model of tricyclic cardiotoxicity

nodes.description: Acidaemia complicating the poisoning. It is not merely a marker here: correcting it is part of treating the cardiac lesion, because a lower pH deepens the channel blockade. Bound to the parent term rather than to Metabolic acidosis, because the cited sources say only "acidosis" and because HPO defines metabolic acidosis as excluding a respiratory cause - which a poisoning that depresses ventilation cannot be assumed to satisfy.

This is where the two channel arms of the poisoning converge, and it is the key conformance target of the xenobiotic-cardiac-channel-perturbation module - the disorder-agnostic step every drug- or toxin-induced channel lesion funnels through, whichever channel was hit and in whichever direction.

nodes.description: Occupancy of the cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel reduces the sodium current that drives phase 0 of the ventricular and Purkinje action potential. The block is rate-dependent - faster pacing means more block - and some drugs of the class leave the channel very slowly, which is why a fast, wide-complex rhythm can be self-sustaining once it starts and why antiarrhythmics that dissociate slowly make it worse. The dissociation rate is drug-specific rather than a class property: amitriptyline is the slow end of the range and imipramine is not.

nodes.description: Widening of the QRS complex on the surface electrocardiogram, the direct reading of slowed intraventricular conduction. It is the most used bedside risk marker in this poisoning: a maximal limb-lead QRS of 100 ms or more marks the exposure at which seizures begin to appear, and 160 ms or more the exposure at which ventricular arrhythmias do. It is a marker of risk rather than a threshold for harm - major complications occur in patients whose QRS is normal.

nodes.description: The standard antidote for the cardiac lesion, given for a widened QRS complex or a ventricular arrhythmia. It works by two separable routes, and experimental work has separated them: raising extracellular sodium increases the driving force through whatever channels remain unblocked, and raising pH shifts the drug toward the un-ionized form that does not bind the channel. Because the second route exists, bicarbonate is worth giving to a cardiotoxic patient whose pH is normal.

nodes.description: An ingested dose large enough that circulating and tissue drug concentrations exceed what the liver can clear, so the drug's several receptor and channel affinities are all expressed at once. Tricyclics are lipophilic and distribute widely, and the same molecule engages the cardiac sodium channel, the hERG potassium channel, alpha-1 adrenergic, muscarinic and histamine H1 receptors, and the neuronal monoamine transporters. Nothing downstream of this node is a metabolite effect or a secondary lesion - they are parallel consequences of one exposure.

evidence.reference_title: Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and targeted temperature management in tricyclic antidepressant-induced cardiac arrest: A case report and literature review.
evidence.snippet: The first-line treatments for patients with hemodynamic instability or wide QRS complex due to TCA-induced cardiotoxicity include fluid resuscitation, sodium bicarbonate administration, vasopressor administration, and antiarrhythmic-agent administration.

nodes.description: Mechanical circulatory support for cardiac arrest or refractory shock that has not responded to fluid, bicarbonate and vasopressors. The argument for it in poisoning is that the lesion is self-limiting - the drug is eventually cleared - so a circulation maintained mechanically for a day or two can bridge to recovery rather than substituting for an organ that will not recover.

evidence.reference_title: Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and targeted temperature management in tricyclic antidepressant-induced cardiac arrest: A case report and literature review.
evidence.snippet: First, VA-ECMO is effective in patients with TCA-induced cardiac arrest.

evidence.reference_title: Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and targeted temperature management in tricyclic antidepressant-induced cardiac arrest: A case report and literature review.
evidence.snippet: VA-ECMO is considered in patients refractory to those interventions.

evidence.reference_title: Management of the cardiovascular complications of tricyclic antidepressant poisoning : role of sodium bicarbonate.
evidence.snippet: Experimental studies suggest extracorporeal circulation membrane oxygenation is also of potential value.

nodes.description: Slowed, heterogeneous conduction supports reentrant circuits in the ventricle. The resulting rhythms are the proximate cause of death in this poisoning, together with the pump failure that arrives with them.

evidence.reference_title: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning.
evidence.snippet: Cardiovascular toxicity is classically manifested as ventricular dysrhythmias, hypotension, heart block, bradyarrhythmias, or asystole.

nodes.description: Disorganized ventricular activity, the terminal rhythm of the reentrant arm.

evidence.reference_title: Can death unrelated to secondary causes be predicted in intubated comatose tricyclic antidepressant-poisoned patients?
evidence.snippet: Ten cases and none of the controls had advanced ECG changes (ventricular fibrillation, torsades des pointes, or asystole).

nodes.description: Monomorphic or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia arising on the reentrant substrate created by slowed conduction. Difficult to distinguish at the bedside from sinus tachycardia with a widened QRS complex, which is the commoner finding.

evidence.reference_title: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning. Management of arrhythmias.
evidence.snippet: Ventricular tachycardia (monomorphic) is a consequence of impaired myocardial depolarisation and impulse conduction.

evidence.reference_title: ECG lead aVR versus QRS interval in predicting seizures and arrhythmias in acute tricyclic antidepressant toxicity.
evidence.snippet: Seizures occurred in 16 patients (20%) and ventricular arrhythmias in 5 (6%).

nodes.description: Dry mouth from muscarinic blockade of salivary secretion.

evidence.reference_title: Poisoning due to tricyclic antidepressant overdosage. Clinical presentation and treatment.
evidence.snippet: The most common clinical features are dry mouth, blurred vision, dilated pupils, sinus tachycardia, pyramidal neurological signs, and drowsiness.

nodes.description: Inhibition of the rapid delayed-rectifier potassium current carried by the hERG channel. Like the sodium channel block, it is use-dependent, so it deepens at the faster rates this poisoning produces.

evidence.reference_title: Blockade of the HERG human cardiac K(+) channel by the antidepressant drug amitriptyline.
evidence.snippet: In rat atrial myocytes bathed in 35 degrees C, 5 microM amitriptyline blocked I(Kr) by 55%.

evidence.reference_title: Blockade of the HERG human cardiac K(+) channel by the antidepressant drug amitriptyline.
evidence.snippet: Block of HERG by amitriptyline was use dependent: exhibiting a much faster block at higher activation frequency.
